newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia sticks to ruble dollar peg.
newsitem.headline: Russia sticks to ruble dollar peg.

text.p: Russia, holding to one of the cornerstones of its anti-inflation policy, Tuesday announced plans to let the ruble decline slowly against the dollar next year and said central bank reserves were adequate to the task.

The sloping corridor, announced by central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin, sets daily target ranges for the ruble between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31. The central bank can invervene on the currency market to defend the ranges.
"We have sufficient (reserves) to carry out the policy which was declared today," Dubinin told the news conference.

The ruble, which rode a roller coaster course in the first years of Russian economic reforms, has been pegged in broad ranges against the dollar since mid-1995, winning cautious trust from Russians who once shunned it in favour of the dollar.
The currency can be freely traded within Russia although capital movements remain restricted. Many of the limits on bringing cash into and out of Russia have been eased.
The ruble traded at around 5,550 to the dollar on Tuesday and the new 1997 policy sets a target range of 5,750-6,350 rubles per dollar by Dec. 31.
Dubinin said the policy would allow the ruble to depreciate by between 0.3 and 1.1 percent a month, in line with expected 1997 monthly inflation rates.
The latest set of bands, also a sloping corridor of daily changing rates, expires in December.
Western economists say the ruble policy has helped bring Russian inflation down sharply because a steady ruble means the prices of imported goods are steady too.
A steady ruble has also reduced inflationary expectations in Russia, where consumer prices rose just 1.2 percent last month. Prices have risen 17.8 percent since the year began.

Finance Minister Alexander Livshits told the news conference that Russia expected a 1997 annual inflation rate of 11.8 percent. "Yesterday's decision of the president, the government and the central bank means that the question of mass issue of money ... is evidently ruled out as a practical policy," he said.
Under the new policy, as under the old one, the central bank will set daily bid and offer rates for the ruble on the interbank market within a 600-point corridor.
